chapters.title: Two paths toward a meeting
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: Come, sit by the fire. A woman has reached the meeting place before her travelling companion. Across the water, the path is still empty. She lifts her bundle: if she leaves now, she can reach home before dark. But if her companion arrives after she has gone, there will be nobody to meet her. The bundle settles against her shoulder. She takes a step, then looks once more toward the bend.

questions.label: Why is she thinking of leaving?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: Home is still a walk away, and the light is going. If she leaves, she can reach it before dark. If she stays, someone may find her waiting.

questions.label: Does this tell my ancestor's journey?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: No ancestor's journey is established here. A fragment can guide curiosity about movement and encounters; it cannot establish anyone's biography.

chapters.title: A region of overlapping lives
chapters.narration: Before 1900, trade linked pastoral Maasai and predominantly agricultural Kikuyu communities around Kiambu; settlement and economic activity overlapped.

choices.label: Stay with the one who waits
Find the one who is late

chapters.title: What a traveller carries onward
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: She chooses to put the bundle down. For a while there is only the water and the fire. Then the missing woman comes round the bend, holding her gourd close. 'I thought you would have gone.' The waiting woman moves her bundle aside. 'I nearly did.' They sit in the space it leaves. When they rise, the path home is darker, but neither follows it alone.

questions.label: What could I ask a relative next?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: You could ask which places or journeys they remember, and whose account each detail comes from. Their answers would remain personal accounts unless separately supported.

chapters.title: A promise still walking
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: On the far side of the water, the late woman is still walking. The path has taken longer than she planned, and the gourd she carries grows heavier with every step. The light is going. If she turns back now, she can send word tomorrow, and nobody will blame her. But a message cannot sit beside someone at dusk. She chooses to keep walking, holding the gourd close, not knowing whether anyone is still there. At the bend she stops. A bundle has been set down by the water, and beside it, a woman is waiting.

questions.label: What could I ask about a journey someone made?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: You could ask what made the journey long, who waited at the other end, and whether word was ever sent ahead. Their answers would remain personal accounts unless separately supported.
